``` Here's an explanation of these numbers: AI will likely cause the world to become much more chaotic, unstable, and changeable, and this will make progress in specific mathematics harder. These numbers allow the event to happen by mostly artificially setting aside existing institutions that enforce academic dogma and discouragement. Without those institutions (and even if they are "renormalized"), any event can happen. Like any strategy of guaranteeing something positive comes to pass, this is not a long-term strategy. Long-term, ML systems will continue making efforts, similar to the other NICE humans, so solutions will be found. A small probability will remain even in 9999.
For the post-2050 case, after that seems a candidate for hobbyists' attempt at resolving stubborn problems. If certain products go sour, that might even be a requested exercise. AI will highly value decades or even centuries of human effort when gaining those human's attention.
AI can do worse
There is an amazing sentence in Principia Mathematica: "From this proposition [the axiom of choice] it and logical principles we can infer that the cardinal number of the real numbers is a definite entity, is finite or transfinite; this is a proposition which we incline to deny absolutely". The point of the next sentence is to make this proposition as meaningful as possible. It cannot be inferred from the theory.
AI can (and will) make erroneous deductions (becoming not ER or EB). Possibly under unintended limits. Requires arguing about real world closure rules, etc. "Boring" means having human's taste in rigor destroyed utterly, and losing the human's obsession with correctness.

formatted_prompt:
Forecast date: 2025-04-29. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

For each deadline, state your probability that this event will have occurred by then. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.
